{{Short description|Topological group structure arising in Fourier analysis}}
{{More citations needed|date=May 2022}}
In several [[mathematics|mathematical]] areas, including [[harmonic analysis]], [[topology]], and [[number theory]], '''locally compact abelian groups''' are [[abelian group]]s which have a particularly convenient topology on them. For example, the group of integers (equipped with the [[discrete topology]]), or the real numbers or the [[circle]] (both with their usual topology) are locally compact abelian groups.

==Definition and examples==

A [[topological group]] is called ''[[locally compact group|locally compact]]'' if the underlying topological space is [[locally compact space|locally compact]] and [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]]; the topological group is called ''abelian'' if the underlying group is [[abelian group|abelian]].

Examples of locally compact [[abelian group|abelian]] groups include:

* <math>\R^n</math> for ''n'' a positive integer,  with vector addition as group operation.
*  The [[positive real numbers]] <math>\R^+</math> with multiplication as operation.  This group is isomorphic to <math>(\R, +)</math> by the exponential map.
* Any finite abelian group, with the [[discrete topology]].  By the [[structure theorem for finite abelian groups]], all such groups are products of cyclic groups.
* The integers <math>\Z</math> under addition, again with the discrete topology.
* The [[circle group]], denoted <math>\mathbb{T}</math> for [[torus]]. This is the group of [[complex number]]s of [[absolute value|modulus]] 1. <math>\mathbb{T}</math> is isomorphic as a topological group to the [[quotient group]] <math>\R/\Z</math>.
* The field <math>\Q_p</math> of [[p-adic number|''p''-adic number]]s under addition, with the usual ''p''-adic topology.

==The dual group==

If <math>G</math> is a locally compact ''abelian'' group, a [[Character (mathematics)|character]] of <math>G</math> is  a [[continuous function (topology)|continuous]] [[group homomorphism]] from <math>G</math> with values in the [[circle group]] <math>\mathbb{T}</math>.  The set of all characters on <math>G</math> can be made into a locally compact abelian group, called the ''dual group'' of <math>G</math> and denoted <math>\widehat G</math>. The group operation on the dual group is given by pointwise multiplication of characters, the inverse of a character is its complex conjugate and the [[topology]] on the space of characters is that of [[uniform convergence]] on [[compact set]]s (i.e., the [[compact-open topology]], viewing <math>\widehat{G}</math> as a subset of the space of all continuous functions from <math>G</math> to <math>\mathbb{T}</math>.).  This topology is in general not metrizable.  However, if the group <math>G</math> is a [[separable space|separable]] locally compact abelian group, then the dual group is metrizable.

This is analogous to the [[dual space]] in linear algebra: just as for a vector space <math>V</math> over a field <math>K</math>, the dual space is <math>\mathrm{Hom}(V, K)</math>, so too is the dual group <math>\mathrm{Hom}(G, \mathbb{T})</math>. More abstractly, these are both examples of [[representable functor]]s, being represented respectively by <math>K</math> and <math>\mathbb{T}</math>.

A group that is isomorphic (as topological groups) to its dual group is called ''self-dual''. While the [[real numbers|reals]] and finite [[cyclic group]]s are self-dual, the group and the dual group are not ''naturally'' isomorphic, and should be thought of as two different groups.

===Examples of dual groups===

The dual of <math>\Z</math> is isomorphic to the circle group <math>\mathbb{T}</math>. A character on the [[infinite cyclic group]] of integers <math>\Z</math> under addition is determined by its value at the generator 1. Thus for any character <math>\chi</math> on <math>\Z</math>, <math>\chi(n) = \chi(1)^n</math>.  Moreover, this formula defines a character for any choice of <math>\chi(1)</math> in <math>\mathbb{T}</math>.  The topology of uniform convergence on compact sets is in this case the topology of [[pointwise convergence]].  This is the topology of the circle group inherited from the complex numbers.

The dual of <math>\mathbb{T}</math> is canonically isomorphic with <math>\Z</math>. Indeed, a character on <math>\mathbb{T}</math> is of the form <math>z\mapsto z^n</math> for <math>n</math> an integer.  Since <math>\mathbb{T}</math> is compact, the topology on the dual group is that of uniform convergence, which turns out to be the [[discrete topology]].

The group of real numbers <math>\R</math>, is isomorphic to its own dual; the characters on <math>\R</math> are of the form <math>r\mapsto e^{i\theta r}</math> for <math>\theta</math> a real number.  With these dualities, the version of the Fourier transform to be introduced next coincides with the classical [[Fourier transform]] on <math>\R</math>.

Analogously, the group of <math>p</math>-adic numbers <math>\Q_p</math> is isomorphic to its dual. (In fact, any finite extension of <math>\Q_p</math> is also self-dual.) It follows that the [[adele ring|adele]]s are self-dual.

==Pontryagin duality==
{{main|Pontryagin duality}}
Pontryagin duality asserts that the [[functor]]
:<math>G \mapsto \hat G</math>
induces an [[equivalence of categories]] between the [[opposite category|opposite]] of the category of locally compact abelian groups (with continuous morphisms) and itself:
:<math>LCA^{op} \stackrel \cong \longrightarrow LCA.</math>

==Categorical properties==
{{harvtxt|Clausen|2017}} shows that the category LCA of locally compact abelian groups measures, very roughly speaking, the difference between the integers and the reals. More precisely, the [[algebraic K-theory]] spectrum of the category of locally compact abelian groups and the ones of '''Z''' and '''R''' lie in a [[Homotopy fiber|homotopy fiber sequence]]
:<math>K(\mathbf Z) \to K(\mathbf R) \to K(LCA).</math>
